newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Canada appeals for landmines ban.
newsitem.headline: Canada appeals for landmines ban.

text.p: Canada appealed on Thursday for a total global ban on anti-personnel landmines in 1997, saying this could be reached most speedily under its own "Ottawa Process".

But Ambassador Mark Moher said Canada would not object to the Conference on Disarmament (CD) starting negotiations to ban the export, import or transfer of landmines -- provided the 61-member forum does not delay concrete results.
The Geneva talks were dominated by the continuing row between Western and non-aligned countries over what its formal negotiating agenda should be in 1997.

Canada, snubbing Britain's proposal last week for the Conference on Disarmament to have a formal negotiating mandate on landmines, said it preferred continuing work in the "Ottawa Process". Some 50 countries take part so far in its talks.
"Anti-personnel (AP) mines constitute a humanitarian and economic scourge with thousands of innocents killed and maimed each year," Moher said in a speech to the Geneva body.

"In our view, use is the problem and it is the use of anti-personnel mines which must be urgently addressed. Thus Canada has set itself a straightforward objective: a legally-binding agreement in 1997 to ban the production, stockpiling, transfer and particularly use of AP mines."
Moher said Canada rejected any suggestion that the Geneva body was the only acceptable mechanism to negotiate a ban.

"If it is the will of this body to pursue the issue of AP mines, we will not oppose it; but we will strongly oppose any initiative which does not reinforce or complement the ongoing work of the Ottawa Process or which delays unduly the establishment of the urgently needed norm against AP mines."

Neither China nor Russia -- two top mine producers and exporters -- take part in the Ottawa talks, although Russia is due to be an observer at a Vienna session next week. "They have strong views on landmines -- they need them," said one envoy.
Many diplomats prefer landmines to be negotiated in the Geneva body, in which both China and Russia are members.
China's position on landmines has been unclear, but Western diplomats expect Ambassador Sha Zukang to return to Geneva at the weekend with fresh instructions.
"China is not wildly enthusiasic about landmines. But we will see what Sha brings," said one Western envoy. I don't think they will block," he added.
Mexico's ambassador said on Thursday that his country opposed negotiating a landmines ban in the Geneva forum.
India, Pakistan and Egypt took the floor to repeat their call for formally establishing an agenda which would include a negotiating committee on total nuclear disarmament.

The five declared nuclear powers (Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States) have made clear they are not ready to negotiate total elimination of their nuclear weapons, but prefer a step-by-step approach starting with fissile material.

Western powers are frustrated with the lack of a consensus to launch negotiations to ban landmines and prohibit production of fissile material (plutonium and highly-enriched uranium), used in nuclear bombs.
"We are trying various ways to resolve things," a U.S. source told Reuters. "It is like a car stuck in snow. We're spinning our wheels, trying to get a grip on something solid to move forward."

Britain's ambassador Sir Michael Weston told Reuters: "It is too early to conclude that we are not going to be able to get down to substantive work. There is a reasonable chance that by the end of next week there will be some clear ideas on how to launch the process and get down to business."
Joon Yung Sun, the South Korean ambassador who currently chairs the talks, has tried to get agreement on an agenda.
"I wish I could provide a panacea, but I am an ordinary man from a small country," he told a news briefing on Tuesday.
